conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how life has felt since your baby arrived. We’re going to use a short, well-trusted tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s just 10 questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything from normal new-mom overwhelm to signs of depression or anxiety that deserve extra care. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll take it one gentle question at a time, and you can answer in your own words; there are no “wrong” answers. Ready to start?

Over the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt—easy, sometimes, not often, or never really?

Um… mostly “sometimes,” I guess. I still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of just feeling tired or worrying that the baby might wake up any second.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes… I can still laugh, but it feels kind of muted, like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it bubbles up naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to—like when my sister mentions grabbing coffee or when my favorite show drops a new episode—but most of the time the feeling fizzles before it actually happens. I’ll think “that sounds nice,” then immediately picture how tired I’ll be or how the baby might need me, and the excitement just sort of drains away.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy and won’t settle, I automatically think I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. Rationally I know babies just have rough patches, but little things still make me feel like I’m failing him somehow, even if it only lasts a few minutes.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly it’s when I’m lying down after a feeding—my mind just starts racing about whether he’s breathing okay, or if that tiny rash is something serious. Nothing’s actually wrong, but the “what-ifs” still pop up and my heart pounds for a bit until I check on him again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of nights this week I’ve woken up suddenly with my heart racing and this tight feeling in my chest. Nothing’s happening—baby’s asleep, the room is quiet—but for a minute or two I feel like something awful is about to happen and I can’t settle myself. It passes, but it’s scary while it’s going on.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days I feel like I’m just one step behind. Dishes pile up, laundry sits, texts go unanswered, and I keep thinking “I’ll catch up at nap-time,” but then I’m either stuck under a sleeping baby or too tired to move. I manage the basics—feeding, diapers, quick shower—but everything else feels like it’s sliding.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s more that I can’t shut my brain off than feeling really unhappy. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, and then lie there running through every little thing—did I wash the bottles, is he gaining enough weight, when will he wake up again? I probably drop off eventually, but it takes a while and I wake up at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some days—like yesterday I just sat on the couch with the baby in my lap and teared up for no real reason. It’s not all day, every day, but little waves of sadness hit me, especially when I’m alone with him and the house is quiet.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not a lot—maybe twice this week. It’s usually when I’m already tired and something small pushes me over, like dropping a pacifier on the floor. I’ll tear up for a minute, wipe my face, and keep going; it’s not an everyday thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My biggest fear is not being enough for the baby, not anything like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant approx. weeks–months old)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [Clinician name, credentials]

Presenting Concerns (self-report)  
• Persistent low/“muted” mood, intermittent tearfulness  
• Markedly reduced enjoyment/anticipation (anhedonia)  
• Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care  
• Intrusive “what-if” worries, nocturnal checking, heart racing  
• Two nocturnal panic episodes (sudden waking, chest tightness)  
• Sleep-onset difficulty linked to racing thoughts; fragmented sleep  
• Daily sense of being overwhelmed; household tasks accumulating  
• Denies any self-harm ideation; protective of infant

Pattern Summary  
Symptoms cluster in depressive (mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt) and anxiety (generalized worry, panic attacks) domains; onset post-delivery, functional impact moderate.

Screening Significance  
– Meets core criteria flagged by Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (low mood items endorsed; items 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 positive).  
– Anxiety symptoms meet clinical threshold for further evaluation.  
– No safety concerns elicited (explicit denial of self-harm thoughts).  
– Risk factors: first-time motherhood, sleep deprivation, perceived social/task overload.

Recommendation  
Continue to full standardized assessment (EPDS, GAD-7, PHQ-9) and consider referral for perinatal mental health evaluation and support services.
